title: Bruising in non-mobile babies and fabricated or induced illness
blurb: Act on any bruise in a baby who is not independently mobile, and recognise the NICE features of fabricated or induced illness.
question: Alfie, 4 months, attends for his immunisations. The practice nurse sees a 1 cm bruise on his cheek. His mother, who seems caring, says his older sister must have poked him. What should the nurse do?

teach.h: Two presentations that are easy to explain away
teach.body: A small bruise on a baby, and a child with puzzling symptoms that never quite add up, are both easily accepted at face value. NICE CG89 says to suspect maltreatment if a child who is not independently mobile has bruising not caused by a medical condition. It also sets out when to consider or suspect fabricated or induced illness (FII), which Working Together 2026 classes as physical abuse. In plain English: 'those who don't cruise rarely bruise', and stories that don't fit the clinical picture need a second look.

teach.caption: Mobile if able to do ANY of: crawl, bottom shuffle, pull to stand, stand unaided, cruise, climb, walk with a push-along walker, walk. Age alone does not decide.

teach.h: Any bruise in a non-mobile baby
teach.body: Bruising or petechiae in a child who is not independently mobile, without a medical cause such as a clotting disorder, should make you suspect maltreatment (CG89 1.1.2). Local bruising protocols require urgent paediatric assessment and a safeguarding referral, whatever the explanation or how caring the parent seems. The paediatric team considers medical causes; the nurse does not decide the cause.
teach.cite: NICE CG89 1.1.2; local safeguarding partnership protocols

teach.h: Bruise in a non-mobile baby: the pathway
teach.caption: Explain to the parent what will happen and why, in a calm, non-accusatory way, unless that would put the baby at risk.

rows.label: Trigger
values: Discrepancy with a recognised clinical picture
Discrepancy plus one or more features below

teach.h: Features that raise suspicion of FII (CG89 1.2.12)
head: Feature
rows: Symptoms appear or reappear when the parent is present
Symptoms reported but observed by the parent alone
New symptoms as soon as old ones resolve
Biologically unlikely history (e.g. big blood loss, not anaemic)
Repeated opinions sought and disputed after a clear diagnosis
Daily life (school, aids) limited beyond the condition
teach.caption: Poisoning: unexpected blood levels of drugs not prescribed for the child should make you suspect maltreatment (CG89 1.2.6).

teach.body: Nurses spend the most time with the child, so their observations matter. Record factually what you see and hear, with times, and what the parent reports, kept separate. Note who was present at each 'episode'. Do not confront the parent or share suspicions with the family before advice, as this may increase risk. Inform the named nurse or safeguarding lead. If you see a child being harmed, ensure their immediate safety and preserve any evidence.

Alfie cannot crawl, shuffle or cruise, so he is not independently mobile. The nurse records the bruise's size, site and colour and the mother's explanation in her words. Following the local bruising protocol, she arranges urgent paediatric assessment and makes a safeguarding referral, telling the mother calmly that this happens for every baby with a bruise. She does not give the immunisations in place of acting on the bruise.

teach.text: A plausible story, a caring parent or a sibling 'poking' do not change the pathway: under the protocol, a bruise in a non-mobile baby goes for urgent paediatric assessment and referral whatever the account. And FII does not exclude real illness: a child with a genuine condition can also be a victim of FII.

items: Not independently mobile = cannot crawl, shuffle, pull to stand, cruise, climb or walk.
Any bruise or petechiae in a non-mobile baby: suspect maltreatment; urgent paediatric assessment and referral.
FII is physical abuse; consider it when the picture does not fit, suspect it with the CG89 features.
Key FII features: symptoms seen by the parent alone, appear when parent present, poor response to treatment, new symptoms as old resolve.
Record factually, don't confront, inform the named nurse; protect the child and preserve evidence if harm is seen.

summary: You can now identify a child who is not independently mobile and follow the bruising pathway without being deflected by explanations. You can also recognise CG89 features of fabricated or induced illness and respond safely as a nurse.

A.q: Maya, 7 months, can roll from front to back and sit when placed, but cannot crawl, shuffle or pull to stand. How should she be classed for the bruising protocol?
options: Independently mobile, as she can roll over
Not independently mobile, as she cannot crawl or shuffle
Independently mobile, as she is over 6 months old
Not independently mobile until she can walk across a room unaided
A.why: CG89 defines mobility as being able to crawl, bottom shuffle, pull to stand, cruise, climb or walk. Rolling and sitting when placed do not count.

whyNot.0: Rolling is not in the CG89 list of independent mobility.
whyNot.2: Age alone does not determine mobility.
whyNot.3: Crawling or cruising is enough; walking is not required.

A.q: A health visitor sees Noor, 3 months, and notices a small bruise on her thigh. Her mother is attentive and says Noor kicked the cot bars. What is the best action?
options: Accept the explanation and review the bruise at the next visit
Ask the GP to see Noor within the week
Advise cot bumpers and record the advice given
Refer for urgent paediatric assessment under the protocol
A.why: Any bruise in a non-mobile baby needs urgent paediatric assessment and safeguarding referral per local protocol, whatever the explanation.

whyNot.0: Accepting the explanation can miss abuse; the protocol applies regardless of account.
whyNot.1: A routine GP appointment within a week is not urgent paediatric assessment.
whyNot.2: Cot advice does not address a possible inflicted injury.

A.q: Toby, 6, has had extensive investigations for reported daily vomiting and 'collapses'. During two weeks on the ward, staff have seen none. Which CG89 feature does this match?
options: Symptoms reported but observed by the parent alone
A history that is biologically unlikely for his age
Repeated opinions sought and disputed
Inexplicably poor response to prescribed treatment
A.why: CG89 1.2.12 lists reported symptoms that are observed by the parent or carer and by nobody else.

whyNot.1: Biologically unlikely refers to histories that cannot fit physiology, such as large blood losses without anaemia.
whyNot.2: Nothing suggests repeated second opinions after a clear diagnosis.

B.q: Grace, 8, is admitted for the fourth time with 'seizures' described by her mother. No episode has been witnessed by staff and video EEG is normal. What is the nurse's most appropriate action?
options: Ask her mother directly whether she is inventing the seizures
Record observations factually and inform the named nurse
Arrange discharge, as the investigations are normal
Start rescue medication in case seizures occur
B.why: Factual records and early advice from the named safeguarding nurse are key. Confronting the parent may increase risk.

whyNot.0: Confronting the parent before advice may put Grace at risk.
whyNot.2: Discharge without addressing the concern leaves the pattern unexplored.
whyNot.3: Treating unwitnessed seizures may cause harm.

B.q: A nurse caring for Ivy, 10 months, who has unexplained faltering growth, walks in and sees her mother drawing feed back out of Ivy's nasogastric tube into a syringe. What should the nurse do first?
options: Ask the mother to explain what she is doing
Leave and report it at the end of the shift
Ensure Ivy's safety, keep the evidence and escalate
Document it and check Ivy's weight again in the morning
B.why: When harm is witnessed, the priority is the child's immediate safety, preserving evidence and escalating at once.

whyNot.0: Questioning first may alert the parent and lose evidence.
whyNot.1: Waiting until the end of the shift leaves Ivy at risk.
whyNot.3: Documentation alone, with delay, fails to protect Ivy.

B.q: Which finding should make a nurse suspect bruising is from maltreatment in a 2-month-old?
options: A bruise with a known clotting disorder
Blue-grey patches recorded at the newborn examination
A raised red birthmark that has grown since birth
Petechiae on the face with no medical cause
B.why: CG89 1.1.2: bruising or petechiae not caused by a medical condition in a non-mobile child should make you suspect maltreatment.

whyNot.0: A clotting disorder is a medical cause.
whyNot.1: Blue-grey patches recorded at birth are congenital dermal melanocytosis, not bruising.
whyNot.2: A growing raised red birthmark is an infantile haemangioma, not a bruise.

C.q: Sami, 11 weeks, attends the ED with a fussy cry. The nurse finds faint bruising on both upper arms. His father, who is calm and helpful, says he holds Sami firmly when changing him. Paediatric review is planned for later. What should the nurse also do?
options: Wait for the paediatric review to decide on referral
Refer to social care under the local bruising protocol
Ask the father to demonstrate how he holds Sami
Advise gentler handling and plan a health visitor review at home
C.why: A non-mobile baby with bruises, especially grip-type bruises on both arms, needs urgent paediatric assessment and a safeguarding referral under the protocol.

whyNot.0: The protocol requires referral alongside assessment, not after it.
whyNot.2: A demonstration does not change the need for referral.
whyNot.3: Handling advice treats an alerting feature as a parenting tip.

C.q: Elsie, 9, has a confirmed diagnosis of asthma. Her mother reports nightly severe attacks never seen on the ward, uses a wheelchair for Elsie, and has sought three further opinions disputing the diagnosis of mild asthma. What is the best interpretation?
options: FII is unlikely, as Elsie has a genuine diagnosis
FII is unlikely, as the mother is seeking help
FII can be excluded once lung function tests are normal
FII should be suspected despite the genuine diagnosis
C.why: Several CG89 1.2.12 features are present (symptoms seen by the parent alone, disputed opinions, aids beyond the condition). FII is likely even with a past or concurrent genuine condition.

whyNot.0: A genuine condition does not exclude FII.
whyNot.1: Seeking help repeatedly can itself be a feature of FII.
whyNot.2: Normal tests do not exclude FII; they may add to the discrepancy.

C.q: A toddler's blood tests show a high level of a sedative that has never been prescribed for her. Her mother has no explanation. What does NICE CG89 advise?
options: Suspect maltreatment and follow safeguarding procedures
Consider maltreatment and repeat the test next week
Consider an accidental ingestion and give safety advice
Suspect a laboratory error and send a repeat sample before acting
C.why: CG89 1.2.6: unexpected blood levels of drugs not prescribed for the child should make you suspect maltreatment.

whyNot.1: This is a 'suspect' feature, and delay risks further harm.
whyNot.2: Without an explanation, accidental ingestion cannot be assumed.

reteach.title: Don't cruise, rarely bruise
reteach.question: Why can't I accept a reasonable explanation for a bruise on a young baby?

blocks.h: Babies who can't move can't bump
blocks.body: A baby who cannot crawl, shuffle or cruise rarely bruises by accident. Even a small bruise can be the first sign of abuse before a much more serious injury. That is why the protocol does not ask whether the story sounds believable: it asks whether the baby is independently mobile. If not, any bruise means urgent paediatric assessment and a referral.

blocks.text: FII: symptoms seen by the parent alone and never by staff are a key warning. A genuine diagnosis does not rule FII out.

explain.body: Mobile if able to crawl, bottom shuffle, pull to stand, stand unaided, cruise, climb, walk with a push-along walker or walk. Under 12 weeks typically not, but age alone does not decide.

test.q: Which ability makes an 8-month-old independently mobile under the CG89 definition?
options: Rolling from back to front
Sitting unsupported when placed on the floor
Bottom shuffling across the floor
Holding the head steady
test.why: Bottom shuffling is listed in the CG89 definition.

whyNot.0: Rolling is not in the list.
whyNot.1: Sitting when placed is not moving from place to place.

explain.body: Any bruise or petechiae in a non-mobile child without a medical cause: suspect maltreatment, urgent paediatric assessment and safeguarding referral per local protocol.

test.q: What makes the bruising protocol apply to a baby?
options: The baby is not independently mobile
The parent's explanation seems unlikely
The bruise is larger than 2 cm across
The family is already known to social care
test.why: The protocol is triggered by bruising in a baby who is not independently mobile, regardless of explanation, size or history.

whyNot.1: The protocol applies even when the explanation seems plausible.

explain.body: Suspect FII when the picture does not fit a recognised condition and, for example, symptoms appear with the parent present, are seen by the parent alone, respond poorly to treatment, or new ones replace resolved ones.

test.q: Which feature is listed by NICE as raising suspicion of FII?
options: The parent asks many detailed questions about the diagnosis
The child is anxious about blood tests
New symptoms are reported as soon as others resolve
The family has travelled far to the hospital
test.why: CG89 1.2.12 includes new symptoms reported as soon as previous ones have resolved.

whyNot.0: Asking questions is normal parental behaviour.
whyNot.1: Anxiety about tests is common in children.
whyNot.3: Travel distance is not a feature.

explain.body: Record factually and separately what is observed and what is reported. Do not confront the parent. Inform the named nurse. If harm is witnessed, protect the child and keep the evidence.

test.q: How should a nurse record a parent's report of an episode that staff did not see?
options: As a witnessed seizure, to keep the records simple and clear
Leave it out, as staff did not see it
Record it as reported by the parent, not observed
Record it as probable fabrication by the parent
test.why: Accurate records distinguish what was reported from what was observed, which is vital in FII assessment.

whyNot.0: Recording it as witnessed is inaccurate.
whyNot.3: Recording an unproven conclusion is not factual.
